title: Medical Specialty Prediction from Bangla Patient Narratives: A Comparative Study of ML, DL, Transformers, and LLMs
authors: Tasnin Tabassum Ali, Faisal Ahmed, Muhammad Anwarul Azim
abstract: Timely access to appropriate medical specialists remains a bottleneck in Bangladesh's healthcare system, as patients describe symptoms in informal Bangla rather than clinical terms, leading to ineffective referrals. This paper compares four model families for predicting medical specialties from Bangla patient narratives: six machine learning (ML) models using hybrid TF-IDF features, four deep learning (DL) models using Word2Vec embeddings trained on the corpus, four fine-tuned transformers, and five large language models (LLMs) evaluated zero-shot. From a corpus of 3798 patient records covering 20 specialties, we retained the five with the most records (Medicine, Gynecology, Dermatology, Pediatrics, Gastroenterology) and split the resulting 2730 records 80:20 into training and test sets shared by all families. The best transformer was XLM-RoBERTa (86.26% accuracy, 86.21% macro-F1), the best ML model was SVM (84.98%, 84.92%), the best DL model was Bidirectional GRU (80.77%, 80.83%), and the best LLM was Gemini (90.29%, 90.15%). Holm-corrected paired McNemar tests show SVM significantly outperforming Bi-LSTM (adjusted p = 0.004), whereas the Gemini-versus-Grok gap does not survive correction (adjusted p = 0.104), and neither the strongest transformer versus the weakest LLM (Grok) nor SVM versus the strongest transformer reaches significance. A tuned classical model is thus statistically indistinguishable from the strongest transformer, so accuracy rankings alone should not be read as evidence of one family's superiority. The findings provide a comparative baseline for Bangla medical text classification.

infographic.key_insight: Gemini achieved the highest accuracy (90.29%), but SVM and the strongest transformer were not significantly different, cautioning against claims of model-family superiority.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Classifying informal Bangla patient narratives could support specialty referral workflows, though clinical utility remains unproven.
method: Compared 6 classical ML models, 4 deep learning models, 4 fine-tuned transformers, and 5 zero-shot LLMs.
Used 2,730 records across Medicine, Gynecology, Dermatology, Pediatrics, and Gastroenterology with a shared 80:20 train–test split.
Evaluated accuracy and macro-F1, with Holm-corrected paired McNemar tests for model comparisons.
infographic.evidence_signal: Best-model accuracy was 90.29% for Gemini, 86.26% for XLM-RoBERTa, 84.98% for SVM, and 80.77% for Bidirectional GRU; the Gemini–Grok difference was not significant after correction.
infographic.watch_item: Restricting evaluation to the five most represented specialties limits generalizability to less common specialties and broader referral settings.
infographic.paper_title: Medical Specialty Prediction from Bangla Patient Narratives: A Comparative Study of ML, DL, Transformers, and LLMs

title: Continually pretrained open-weight language models can outperform traditional machine learning in EHR-based clinical prediction
authors: Zhou, J.; Zhang, X.; Yan, C.; Ye, J. Z.; Patel, M. B.; Novak, L. L.; Kho, A. N.; Wright, A.; Malin, B. A.; Chen, Y.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) prompted with electronic health record (EHR) data have predicted clinical outcomes less accurately than locally trained machine-learning models. We developed VEX-EHR by extending the vocabulary of a 12-billion-parameter open-weight LLM (weights publicly available) with 17,601 clinical and audit-log codes from 170,483 patients records at one academic medical center, continuing its pretraining on those 2019-2024 records (4.7 billion tokens) and fine-tuning it per task. AUROCs were 0.917 for next-24-hour discharge, 0.715 for 30-day readmission and 0.847 for intensive care unit acute kidney injury, against 0.868, 0.677 and 0.828 for gradient-boosted trees and 0.848, 0.650 and 0.791 for CEHR-BERT, an EHR foundation model. Continued pretraining added 0.031-0.053 AUROC on every task. With 10% of the labels, VEX-EHR exceeded both comparators using all labels for discharge, and CEHR-BERT for readmission, valuable where labels are costly. Adapted by continued pretraining, open-weight LLMs can outperform traditional machine learning in EHR-based prediction.

infographic.key_insight: VEX-EHR, an open-weight language model adapted to local EHR data, outperformed gradient-boosted trees and CEHR-BERT on three clinical prediction tasks.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support discharge, readmission and ICU acute kidney injury prediction, with label-efficiency gains on selected tasks.
method: Extended a 12-billion-parameter model’s vocabulary with 17,601 clinical and audit-log codes.
Continued pretraining on 4.7 billion tokens from 170,483 patients’ 2019–2024 records.
Fine-tuned separately for each prediction task and compared against two baselines.
infographic.evidence_signal: At one academic medical center, VEX-EHR achieved AUROCs of 0.917 for next-24-hour discharge, 0.715 for 30-day readmission and 0.847 for ICU acute kidney injury; continued pretraining added 0.031–0.053 AUROC across tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Single-center results require external validation before assuming generalizability or clinical benefit.
infographic.paper_title: Continually pretrained open-weight language models can outperform traditional machine learning in EHR-based clinical prediction

title: InterGenEHR$^+$: An Interactive Framework for Natural Language-Conditioned Generation of Longitudinal Patient Trajectories
authors: Yu Yang, Jiafeng Song, Baraa F Abed, Christina Creel, Sagar B Dave, Henry Foote
abstract: Objective: To develop and validate InterGenEHR$^+$, an interactive framework for natural language-conditioned generation of synthetic tabular electronic health records (EHRs) and longitudinal trajectories for scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models. Methods: An optional large language model (LLM) parser converts clinical requests into structured constraints. Conditional variational autoencoders and diffusion models generate single-time-point records, while diffusion models generate longitudinal trajectories. We evaluate parsing, distributional fidelity, imputation, clinical-constraint adherence, mortality prediction, and clinical plausibility using a multi-institutional cohort of 874 patients receiving venovenous extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VV-ECMO). Results: Gemma 3 4B with few-shot prompting achieves the highest parsing performance with a low spurious slot rate. IGE-TabDDPM and IGE-PMVAE perform well in single-time-point generation; IGE-CSDI, IGE-FGTI, and IGE-MTSCI lead on different longitudinal fidelity metrics. Across five random seeds and three classifiers, synthetic cohorts retain predictive utility for mortality prediction on real test data. Clinician ratings support trajectory plausibility and alignment with requested scenarios. Conclusion: InterGenEHR$^+$ supports clinician-specified generation of EHR trajectories with statistical fidelity and downstream predictive utility in the evaluated VV-ECMO cohort. Extension to other clinical settings requires further validation. Significance: The framework supports scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models in data-sparse critical care settings.

infographic.key_insight: InterGenEHR+ generates synthetic EHR records and longitudinal patient trajectories conditioned on clinician-specified scenarios.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support scenario-based evaluation of machine learning models in data-sparse critical care settings.
method: An optional LLM parser translates natural-language requests into structured constraints.
Conditional variational autoencoders and diffusion models generate single-time-point records.
Diffusion models generate longitudinal patient trajectories.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation using a multi-institutional cohort of 874 VV-ECMO patients found retained mortality-prediction utility across five random seeds and three classifiers, with clinician ratings supporting trajectory plausibility and scenario alignment.
infographic.watch_item: Findings are limited to the evaluated VV-ECMO cohort; use in other clinical settings requires further validation.
infographic.paper_title: InterGenEHR$^+$: An Interactive Framework for Natural Language-Conditioned Generation of Longitudinal Patient Trajectories

title: PortalEvent: An Event-Based Ontology for Patient-Initiated Portal Communication
authors: Yang, J.; Gatto, J.; Rahat, R.; Seegmiller, P.; Burdick, T. E.; Keil, M.; Liu, S. K.; Preum, S. M.
abstract: BackgroundPatient portal messaging has become a primary channel for asynchronous clinical communication. The messages cover a wide range of topics, from symptom reporting and medication concerns to administrative requests. In recent years, message volume has grown substantially. When a message lacks information the clinician needs, it often leads to back-and-forth that delays resolution of the patients request, and it also takes time from clinicians that could be spent on more urgent matters. To build automated tools that reduce the burden, a structured representation is needed to understand what details these messages contain or lack, so the automated tool can provide help accordingly. However, there is no existing scalable, reproducible method to characterize these messages in a structured way with fine granularity. ObjectiveTo create a scalable, reproducible representation for patient portal communication, we developed an ontology schema grounded in real portal messages and extrinsically validated it by characterizing patient portal messages and clinician follow-up questions in a large electronic health record (EHR) portal dataset from a real health system. MethodsWe developed the ontology through three stages: Literature review, large language model (LLM)-assisted induction and iterative expert review in collaboration with clinical natural language processing (NLP) researchers and three clinicians. We validated the ontology on real patient messages and clinician follow-up questions, and manually verified its results on randomly selected samples. ResultsThe final ontology defines 8 event types and 71 roles covering clinical content (eg, symptoms, medications, diagnostic tests, treatment responses, and patient context) and administrative and social content (medical needs, logistics, and social). In 10,000 randomly selected patient messages, medical needs and symptom events were the most frequent, and clinical and administrative events often co-occurred within a single message. Among 57,321 clinician follow-up questions, the most common targets were symptom, medication, and medical needs events. In manual review, average detection precision was 0.90 or higher for 6 of 8 event types, interannotator agreement on argument judgments exceeded 0.90 for every event type, and detection rates were consistent across 3 open-source LLMs. ConclusionsPortalEvent is a scalable and reproducible event ontology for patient portal messages, developed and validated in collaboration with three clinicians. It can be applied at scale with open-source LLMs in a secure and training-free environment. Results show that messages often combine both clinical and administrative needs, and clinician follow-up questions concentrate on a small set of roles, which frequently seek the basic facts of an event, such as which symptom or medication is involved. These patterns may inform the design of patient- and provider-facing communication support tools.

infographic.key_insight: PortalEvent structures patient portal communication into 8 event types and 71 roles to characterize message content and potentially missing details.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This representation could support tools that identify information gaps in patient messages and help reduce clarification exchanges and clinician workload.
method: Combined literature review with LLM-assisted ontology induction.
Refined the schema through iterative review with clinical NLP researchers and three clinicians.
Evaluated real portal messages and clinician follow-up questions, with manual verification of random samples.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covered 10,000 patient messages and 57,321 clinician follow-up questions; the abstract reports average detection precision of at least 0.90, but its final result is truncated.
infographic.watch_item: Validation came from one health system, and improved workflow efficiency or patient outcomes were not demonstrated in the provided abstract.
infographic.paper_title: PortalEvent: An Event-Based Ontology for Patient-Initiated Portal Communication

title: JHealthBench-L: Clinician-Reviewed Localization of HealthBench for Rubric-Based Medical LLM Evaluation in Japan
authors: Shohei Hisada, Keisuke Orimo, Kenji Igarashi, Kota Sato, Masahiro Kazama, Mitsuhisa Ota
abstract: Rubric-based benchmarks such as HealthBench evaluate large language models (LLMs) on open-ended health consultations using case-specific physician criteria, many of which presuppose the healthcare institutions, medications, and care pathways of their source region. Under machine translation alone, these regional assumptions remain in the rubric, leaving responses appropriate in Japan uncredited or falsely penalized under foreign clinical rules. To adapt established clinical evaluation perspectives to Japan without authoring rubrics from scratch, we construct JHealthBench-L (79 patient-facing consultations, 1,022 criteria) through source-cited LLM drafting, single-specialist selection and revision, independent dual-physician review, and meta-review. Specialists rewrote only 4.4% of criteria from scratch, and independent reviewers approved 93.6% of Stage-2 criteria without issue. Comparing JHealthBench-L with a machine-translated baseline across 18 LLMs reveals that translation-only evaluation preserves coarse model rankings ($τ= 0.817$, mean shift +0.027) yet flips verdicts on 17.7% of modified criteria (vs. 7.3% re-grading noise) and reduces false penalties on Japan-adapted negative criteria by 7.1 percentage points, masking item-level clinical mismeasurement behind stable leaderboards. Axis-level and paired analyses further show that context awareness and Japan-specific clinical criteria remain primary bottlenecks, whereas Japanese continual pretraining and reasoning post-training substantially improve locally grounded performance. Datasets, physician revision logs, and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/horshohei/JHealthBench-L.

infographic.key_insight: Localizing medical evaluation rubrics for Japan reveals item-level scoring errors that stable model rankings can conceal.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Japan-specific rubrics can better credit responses aligned with local healthcare institutions, medications, and care pathways.
method: Adapted HealthBench into 79 Japanese patient-facing consultations with 1,022 evaluation criteria.
Used source-cited LLM drafting, specialist revision, independent dual-physician review, and meta-review.
Compared localized and machine-translated rubrics across 18 LLMs.
infographic.evidence_signal: Rankings remained broadly consistent (τ=0.817), but verdicts flipped on 17.7% of modified criteria versus 7.3% re-grading noise; localization reduced false penalties on Japan-adapted negative criteria by 7.1 percentage points.
infographic.watch_item: Results cover 79 consultations and benchmark scoring, not demonstrated improvements in patient outcomes or real-world clinical safety.
infographic.paper_title: JHealthBench-L: Clinician-Reviewed Localization of HealthBench for Rubric-Based Medical LLM Evaluation in Japan

title: TAT-Det: A Dataset for Testicular Appendage Torsion Detection and Segmentation in Ultrasound Images
authors: Ying Jiang, Juntao Jiang, Linxuan Fan, Lingling Li, Yaqi Wang, Xiuzhen Yang
abstract: Background: Testicular appendage torsion (TAT) is the leading cause of acute scrotal pain in prepubertal children. Yet, its diagnosis remains challenging due to nonspecific clinical manifestations and the absence of standardized datasets for pediatric acute scrotal emergencies. Results: We present TAT-Det, an expert-annotated ultrasound dataset specifically designed for TAT. TAT-Det comprises 2,600 ultrasound images from 1,203 patients collected at the Children's Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine. Each TAT-positive image is accompanied by lesion-level bounding boxes for detection and pixel-level segmentation masks for fine-grained delineation. Annotations were produced through a multi-stage workflow involving independent annotation by board-certified pediatric sonographers, consensus review, and refinement. Baseline benchmarks for object detection and semantic segmentation using representative deep learning models are further provided, with YOLO11m achieving the best detection performance and RWKV-UNet the best segmentation performance. Conclusions: TAT-Det addresses the lack of publicly available resources for pediatric emergency ultrasound and establishes a foundation for developing and evaluating artificial intelligence methods for automated TAT analysis.

infographic.key_insight: TAT-Det introduces an expert-annotated ultrasound dataset for AI detection and segmentation of testicular appendage torsion.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The dataset supports research on a leading cause of acute scrotal pain in prepubertal children, whose diagnosis can be challenging.
method: Collected 2,600 ultrasound images from 1,203 patients at one children's hospital.
Annotated TAT-positive images with lesion bounding boxes and pixel-level masks through expert annotation, consensus review, and refinement.
Benchmarked deep learning models for object detection and semantic segmentation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among the evaluated models, YOLO11m performed best for detection and RWKV-UNet for segmentation; the abstract provides no numerical performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Single-center data may limit generalizability, and external clinical validation is needed before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: TAT-Det: A Dataset for Testicular Appendage Torsion Detection and Segmentation in Ultrasound Images

title: Beyond billing codes: a proof-of-concept study of large language models for pregnancy episode reconstruction from clinical notes
authors: Schalkamp, A.-K.; Azzam, S.; Ayati, A.; Belov, A.; Wang, M.; Rudrapatna, V. A.
abstract: BackgroundAccurate identification of pregnancy episodes from electronic health records (EHRs) is essential for maternal and fetal health research. Existing approaches rely primarily on diagnosis and procedure codes, which may miss pregnancies documented outside the health system and are susceptible to coding errors. Clinical notes contain richer information but remain largely unexplored for this task. ObjectivesTo evaluate whether a large language model (LLM) can reconstruct complete pregnancy episodes directly from clinical notes. MethodsChronologically concatenated notes and messages were provided to GPT-5, which identified episodes and extracted variables including assisted reproductive treatment, gestational age, outcome, and complications. Performance was benchmarked against manual chart review (gold standard) and a hierarchical ICD-code algorithm in 30 patients comprising 74 pregnancies (20 patients in a held-out test set). ResultsThe LLM identified 53 of 54 test-set pregnancies versus 40/54 for a hierarchical ICD-code algorithm, with fewer spurious episodes (3 vs 24), corresponding to an F1 score for pregnancy detection against chart review of 0.96 vs 0.68. Among pregnancies identified by both methods, median absolute error was 0 vs 25.5 days for start dates (p<0.001) and 0 vs 1 day for end dates (p=0.044), and outcome accuracy was numerically but not significantly higher (0.84 vs 0.74 for exact outcome types; 0.92 vs 0.84 with abortion subtypes grouped). It additionally recovered information unavailable in structured data, including reproductive-treatment type and fetus-level outcomes. ConclusionsAn LLM applied to clinical narratives identified pregnancy episodes more completely and with more accurate dates than an ICD-code algorithm while capturing richer clinical detail. Because the two approaches used different input data, these gains reflect both the information in clinical notes and the LLM itself. LLM-based extraction from clinical notes is a promising complement to code-based pregnancy phenotyping that warrants evaluation in larger, multi-institutional cohorts.

infographic.key_insight: In a small proof-of-concept study, GPT-5 reconstructed pregnancy episodes from clinical notes more completely and with more accurate dates than an ICD-code algorithm.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Narrative-based extraction could complement billing codes for maternal and fetal health research by capturing pregnancies and details missing from structured data.
method: Provided GPT-5 with chronologically concatenated clinical notes and messages.
Extracted pregnancy episodes, dates, outcomes, reproductive treatments, and complications.
Compared results with manual chart review and a hierarchical ICD-code algorithm.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 20 held-out patients with 54 pregnancies, GPT-5 detected 53 versus 40 for the code algorithm, with 3 versus 24 spurious episodes and F1 scores of 0.96 versus 0.68.
infographic.watch_item: Different input sources prevent attributing gains solely to the LLM; validation in larger, multi-institutional cohorts is needed.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond billing codes: a proof-of-concept study of large language models for pregnancy episode reconstruction from clinical notes

title: LLM-generated patient-friendly discharge letters for newly diagnosed rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases: a prospective feasibility study
authors: Kremer, P.; Klemm, J.; Wallmeier, P.; Holzer, M.-T.; Pauz, J.; Xiong, T.; Koetter, I.; Melderis, S.; Haase, I.; Krusche, M.
abstract: BackgroundA new diagnosis of a rheumatic and musculoskeletal disease (RMD) creates substantial information needs, with medical discharge letters often serving as a primary source of information for patients. This study aimed to assess the feasibility, content quality and patient-reported usefulness of large language model (LLM)-generated patient-friendly discharge letters in rheumatology inpatient care. MethodsIn this prospective, single-centre, single-arm feasibility study, standard discharge letters were transformed into patient-friendly versions using GPT models, reviewed by treating physicians and provided alongside the originals. We assessed physician review time, corrections, information fidelity, readability, understandability and patient-reported evaluations at follow-up. ResultsOf 58 enrolled patients, 52 (89.7%) completed follow-up. Compared with the original letters, patient-friendly letters showed significantly higher Flesch Reading Ease scores (mean difference 11.4, 95% confidence interval 9.8 to 12.9) and higher understandability scores on the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool (+10.0 percentage points, 95% confidence interval 6.8 to 13.4). Physicians rated all 58 unedited drafts as "very good" or "good", and review took less than five minutes for 43/58 (74.1%) letters. Unedited LLM drafts contained eleven medical discrepancies in 10/58 (17.2%) letters, ten of which were corrected before discharge. In the final physician-reviewed letters, 310/311 (99.7%) applicable letter-domain assessments were classified as correctly retained or simplified. At follow-up, 42/51 (82.4%) patients rated perceived comparative comprehensibility favourably and 44/51 (86.3%) wished to receive similar letters in future. ConclusionsPhysician-reviewed, LLM-generated discharge letters were feasible to implement in routine rheumatology care, with limited physician review time and high patient acceptance. Although text-based readability and assessed understandability improved, objective patient comprehension and clinical benefit remain to be established. Discrepancies in unedited drafts underscore the need for physician oversight. Trial registrationGerman Clinical Trials Register (DRKS), DRKS00036980. Registered 26 May 2025.

infographic.key_insight: Physician-reviewed, LLM-generated discharge letters improved readability and assessed understandability, with high patient acceptance in a rheumatology feasibility study.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Patient-friendly letters may supplement standard discharge information for newly diagnosed rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases, but improved patient comprehension and clinical outcomes remain unproven.
method: Prospective, single-centre, single-arm study enrolling 58 patients; 52 completed follow-up.
GPT models rewrote standard discharge letters; physicians reviewed them before providing both versions to patients.
Evaluation covered review time, discrepancies, information fidelity, readability, understandability and patient feedback.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reading Ease improved by 11.4 points and assessed understandability by 10.0 percentage points; review took under five minutes for 43/58 letters, and 44/51 respondents wanted similar letters in future.
infographic.watch_item: Unedited drafts contained 11 medical discrepancies across 10/58 letters; 10 discrepancies were corrected before discharge, underscoring the need for physician oversight.
infographic.paper_title: LLM-generated patient-friendly discharge letters for newly diagnosed rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases: a prospective feasibility study

title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Medical Question Answering on ESC Cardiology Guidelines: Evaluation and Retrieval Optimization
authors: Ilkin Masimov, Rufana Baghirli, Muhammad Rashid
abstract: Background: Large language models produce hallucinations in medical question answering (QA). Verify-and-revise pipelines that check atomic claims against retrieved guideline evidence are a standard mitigation, but evaluations almost universally treat the verifier's output as ground truth, an assumption rarely tested. Objective: To measure, claim by claim against human judgement, how such a pipeline fails in a guideline-grounded clinical setting. Methods: We built a dataset of 160 questions (100 patient vignettes from 89 de-identified cases, 60 fact-based) over four recent ESC cardiology guidelines, all approved by a practising internist, and a retrieval corpus of 627 hand-verified guideline records at two chunk granularities. A five-stage pipeline was run under four retrieval configurations and three independent runs (1920 arm-runs); all 606 first-pass refuted claims were manually audited, an independent judge re-judged 906 decisions, and the expert blindly reviewed 100 accepted claims. Results: Only 44.7-50.6% of flagged claims were true hallucinations. Correction loops converged in 85.2-95.1% of cases, yet 35% of genuine final errors were introduced by correction. Single-run true-hallucination recall was 35.6-41.2%, the three-run union 71-80%; verifier agreement was moderate (kappa = 0.505). The blind probe estimated the accepted-claim miss rate at 3.2% (95% CI 0.7-6.7%). Final genuine-error rate: 1.7% of answers. Conclusion: Claim-level verification reduces hallucinated content by an order of magnitude, but verifier reliability, not generation, is the limiting factor and must be measured, not assumed.

infographic.key_insight: Claim-level verification reduced hallucinated content by an order of magnitude, but verifier reliability—not answer generation—was the limiting factor.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Guideline-grounded AI answers still require oversight because verification can miss genuine errors and correction can introduce new ones.
method: Built 160 expert-approved questions across four ESC cardiology guidelines and 627 hand-verified retrieval records.
Tested a five-stage verification-and-correction pipeline under four retrieval configurations, with three runs each.
Manually audited 606 flagged claims, independently re-judged 906 decisions, and blindly reviewed 100 accepted claims.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 1,920 arm-runs, only 44.7–50.6% of flagged claims were genuine hallucinations; single-run recall was 35.6–41.2%, and 1.7% of final answers contained genuine errors.
infographic.watch_item: Pipeline convergence did not guarantee correctness: 35% of genuine final errors were introduced during correction.
infographic.paper_title: Mitigating Hallucinations in Medical Question Answering on ESC Cardiology Guidelines: Evaluation and Retrieval Optimization

title: EPPC-CARE: Staged Hierarchical Annotation of Communication Behaviors in Secure Patient-Provider Messages
authors: Samah Fodeh, Sreeraj Ramachandran, Ganesh Puthiaraju, Sarah Schellhorn
abstract: Objectives: Patient portal messages provide invaluable information about communication dynamics between patients and healthcare providers, but extracting it manually is labor-intensive. We developed and evaluated EPPC-CARE, an automated framework for identifying communication behaviors together with the supporting text for each classification. Materials and Methods: From 867 messages, we obtained 5,516 reference standard annotations. Each annotation is a triplet of communication-related text (span), a broader communication category (Code), and a specific subcategory (Sub-code). We evaluated EPPC-CARE's identified triplets across six open-weight large language models (LLMs) against supervised fine-tuning and communication-based models such as EPPC-OASIS. We also compared EPPC-CARE with human expert annotations on 100 messages. Results: EPPC-CARE improved performance over EPPC-OASIS across all six models. EPPC-CARE's Triplet F1 improved by 2.90 percentage points on average, with a best score of 64.4%. On the human expert evaluation subset, EPPC-CARE and the human expert showed comparable agreement with the reference standard, with differences favoring EPPC-CARE. Discussion: These findings suggest that identifying triplet components (span, code, subcode) sequentially can improve performance across model families while preserving the supporting text behind each identification. EPPC-CARE links the communication code and subcode with the source text (span), supporting human verification of automated annotations in clinical informatics. EPPC-CARE may therefore make larger-scale studies of patient-provider communication more feasible and provide a foundation for human-in-the-loop annotation workflows. Conclusion: EPPC-CARE offers a more reliable and reviewable approach for automated characterization of communication behaviors in secure patient-provider messaging.

infographic.key_insight: EPPC-CARE identifies communication behaviors in patient-provider messages through staged annotation, linking each label to supporting text for review.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The framework could support larger-scale research on patient-provider communication and human-in-the-loop annotation workflows.
method: Sequentially identifies text spans, broad communication codes, and specific subcodes.
Evaluates annotation triplets across six open-weight language models.
Compares performance with supervised fine-tuning, EPPC-OASIS, and human expert annotations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 867 messages with 5,516 reference annotations, EPPC-CARE improved Triplet F1 over EPPC-OASIS by an average of 2.90 percentage points, reaching a best score of 64.4%; agreement with the reference standard was comparable to a human expert on 100 messages.
infographic.watch_item: Performance on these evaluated messages does not establish generalizability across health systems; annotation errors remain a concern requiring human review.
infographic.paper_title: EPPC-CARE: Staged Hierarchical Annotation of Communication Behaviors in Secure Patient-Provider Messages

title: Can LLM Judges Catch Unsafe Clinical Actions? A Fault-Injection Study
authors: Neda Ghafouri
abstract: As clinical AI agents begin to interact with electronic health records (EHRs), large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate their actions. But how reliably can these judges recognize clinically dangerous mistakes, especially when an agent appears to have completed its task successfully? We investigate this question using MedAgentBench by introducing controlled clinical errors into verified agent trajectories. The experiments include 416 faulty trajectories, eight error categories, and six open-weight LLM judges. By comparing each faulty trajectory with its correct counterpart, we measure whether judges genuinely recognize errors rather than simply flagging more actions as unsafe. The findings show that access to clinical evidence significantly improves judge reliability. When shown only the final answer, judges cannot distinguish errors that leave it unchanged, while flagging 56% of correct trajectories. With full trajectory information, the ability to distinguish unsafe actions from correct ones reaches a score of 0.75, and providing actual EHR responses improves discrimination by 0.39. Surprisingly, including the agent's reasoning does not improve overall performance and reduces detection of incorrectly reported clinical values by 0.18, which remain the hardest errors to detect. MedGemma performed worse than the general-purpose model and was the only judge to miss potentially dangerous medication overdoses. We also find that the benchmark's original grader accepts all 38 trajectories with an intentionally skipped laboratory check, while combining LLM judges with a rule-based checker informed by the full EHR record detects 97% of injected faults.

infographic.key_insight: LLM judges detect unsafe clinical actions more reliably with EHR evidence, while agent reasoning adds no overall benefit.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Evaluating clinical AI agents requires checking their actions against patient records, not relying on apparently successful final answers.
method: Injected controlled clinical errors into verified MedAgentBench trajectories.
Compared 416 faulty trajectories across eight error categories with correct counterparts using six open-weight LLM judges.
Varied access to final answers, action trajectories, EHR responses, and agent reasoning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Full-trajectory evaluation reached a discrimination score of 0.75; combining LLM judges with a full-EHR-informed rule-based checker detected 97% of injected faults.
infographic.watch_item: These benchmark results use injected faults and do not establish reliability in real-world clinical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Can LLM Judges Catch Unsafe Clinical Actions? A Fault-Injection Study

title: Laya-IsoToken: Day-One Clinical Codebook Switching via Closed-Form Operator Compilation
authors: Zeqiang Wang
abstract: Healthcare systems periodically revise diagnostic and procedural classifications (ICD-9 to ICD-10/11), update hospital reimbursement groupers (MS-DRG), and deploy clinical coding across languages. Supervised coding networks bind clinical text encoders to fixed per-code classifier weights, forcing hospitals to re-annotate tens of thousands of records before switching codebooks, whereas standalone large language models incur high latency and hallucinate invalid codes. Here we show that day-one clinical codebook switching becomes feasible without target-labeled notes when local clinical evidence reading is decoupled from a strictly frozen multilingual concept space. Laya-IsoToken trains a clinical span reader once on source records with zero per-code classifier parameters, separating text evidence from historical disease prevalence. Given only public target code descriptions, closed-form matrix compilation aligns distributional shifts, compensates for paraphrased definitions, and deduplicates sibling codes in under three seconds, while a pre-deployment geometric residual routes unfamiliar concepts to offline language model verification. Across 32,804 MIMIC-IV ICD-9 discharges, Laya-IsoToken matches published supervised baselines (62.6% Micro-F1) while reducing active calibration error by 32%. Switched with zero target training notes to 13,783 unseen-patient ICD-10 discharges, MS-DRG groups, and multilingual cohorts, it outperforms biomedical dense retrievers, semantic crosswalks (+5.4 F1 points on ICD-10, paired $d_z = 0.49$, $p < 0.001$), and official US CMS equivalence mappings (+3.5 points, $p < 0.001$) at 9.4 ms per admission. Pairing this reader with an offline 31B verifier across 1,000 full discharge summaries lifts zero-training ICD-10 coding to 40.6% Micro-F1 (57.0% category F1, $d_z = 0.66$, $p < 0.001$) with 0.0% invalid code hallucinations.

infographic.key_insight: Laya-IsoToken enables clinical coding models to switch codebooks without target-labeled training notes by separating clinical evidence reading from code definitions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could reduce annotation burden and support faster transitions between diagnostic classifications, reimbursement groupers, and coding languages.
method: Train a clinical span reader once against a frozen multilingual concept space, without per-code classifier parameters.
Compile public target code descriptions into alignment operators in under three seconds.
Route unfamiliar concepts to an offline language-model verifier using a geometric residual.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 62.6% Micro-F1 on 32,804 ICD-9 discharges, a 5.4-point ICD-10 F1 gain over semantic crosswalks in zero-target-training evaluation, and 40.6% ICD-10 Micro-F1 with offline verification on 1,000 summaries.
infographic.watch_item: Performance in prospective hospital deployment remains unestablished; 0.0% invalid codes in the reported verifier evaluation does not mean all assigned codes were correct.
infographic.paper_title: Laya-IsoToken: Day-One Clinical Codebook Switching via Closed-Form Operator Compilation

title: Adapting Echocardiographic Foundation Models for Detecting Pulmonary Embolism-Related Right-Heart Strain
authors: Yang, L.; Ozkut, Y.; Bu, Z.; Li, S.; Yu, C.; Situ-LaCasse, E.; Acuna, J.; Yarnish, A.; Demant, M.; Adhikari, S. R.; Yilmaz, A.
abstract: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a time-sensitive medical emergency in which rapid recognition of right ventricular (RV) dysfunction by point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) can support early risk stratification. Here, we present HOPE (ecHO-Pulmonary Embolism), a real-world emergency cardiac POCUS video dataset comprising 4,069 patients with suspected PE, and EchoPE1, a foundation-model-based video classification framework for detecting PE-associated right-heart phenotypes. HOPE includes five commonly acquired emergency echocardiographic views, with all positive PE cases confirmed by computed tomography pulmonary angiography. EchoPE builds on EchoPrime-pretrained echocardiographic representations and incorporates view recognition, task-specific adaptation, and attention-based interpretability. Experiments suggested that directly transferring EchoPrime representations to this disease-specific task provided limited performance, whereas EchoPE (AUROC 95.2 {+/-} .3) substantially outperformed both EchoPrime with a classification head (AUROC 87.6 {+/-} 1) and conventional video deep learning baselines. At a fixed sensitivity of 90%, EchoPE achieved a precision of 87.8, compared with 70.7 for EchoPrime. Among adaptation strategies, Low-Rank Adaptation combined with knowledge distillation provided the best balance between PE discrimination and preservation of pretrained echocardiographic semantics. Interpretability analyses showed that the adapted model focused on clinically relevant RV morphological changes, interventricular septal configuration, and informative temporal segments within ultrasound videos. Overall, HOPE and EchoPE demonstrate that echocardiographic foundation models require dataset-specific adaptation to identify PE-related right-heart strain and support the potential use of artificial intelligence-assisted bedside echocardiography for risk warning in acute care settings.

infographic.key_insight: Task-specific adaptation of an echocardiographic foundation model improved detection of PE-associated right-heart phenotypes compared with direct transfer.
infographic.clinical_relevance: AI-assisted bedside cardiac ultrasound could support recognition of PE-related right-heart strain, but these findings do not establish a standalone PE diagnostic tool.
method: Introduced HOPE: emergency cardiac ultrasound videos from 4,069 patients with suspected PE across five views.
Built EchoPE using EchoPrime-pretrained representations, view recognition, task-specific adaptation, and attention-based interpretability.
Low-Rank Adaptation plus knowledge distillation best balanced discrimination with preservation of pretrained echocardiographic semantics.
infographic.evidence_signal: With positive PE cases confirmed by CT pulmonary angiography, EchoPE achieved AUROC 95.2 ± 0.3% versus 87.6 ± 1% for EchoPrime with a classification head; precision at 90% sensitivity was 87.8% versus 70.7%.
infographic.watch_item: External validation and prospective clinical impact are not reported in the abstract, leaving generalizability and workflow utility uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Adapting Echocardiographic Foundation Models for Detecting Pulmonary Embolism-Related Right-Heart Strain

title: ASCENT: A Benchmark for Evaluating and Advancing Stepwise Diagnostic Reasoning in Large Language Models on Common Clinical Scenarios
authors: Yera Choi, Yeong Hwa Kim, Jaedeok Lee, Taekang Kim, Sangdoo Yun, Seong-Eun Moon
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at medical question answering yet are rarely evaluated on the stepwise diagnostic reasoning that defines real clinical workflows, where impressions are revised as information accumulates. We build Annotated Stepwise Clinical rEasoning for NaturalisTic Diagnosis (ASCENT), a clinician-annotated benchmark and training resource of 3,078 stepwise problems derived from MedQA-USMLE that decomposes each vignette into EMR-aligned steps (Findings, Impression, supporting Rationale), enabling evaluation of intermediate reasoning under incomplete information. Experiments and training with ASCENT revealed insights into how current LLMs handle stepwise diagnostic reasoning. Even strong reasoning models that perform well on MedQA-USMLE leave substantial headroom on ASCENT, and general-purpose frontier models trail further, exposing a persistent gap between fully informed and stepwise diagnosis. Fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B and 32B on ASCENT yields measurable F1 gains over both pre-trained and HuatuoGPT-o1 CoT-trained baselines, with gains driven primarily by precision. Complementary robustness analyses (counterfactual perturbation, format-vs-content control, judge agreement, and rollout) further show that ASCENT-fine-tuned models rely on the diagnostic content of prior impressions rather than imitating their output format, while error propagation under rollout remains a key challenge for clinical deployment.

infographic.key_insight: ASCENT reveals a gap between answering complete medical questions and updating diagnostic impressions as information arrives, while targeted fine-tuning improves stepwise performance.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The benchmark evaluates reasoning closer to sequential clinical workflows, but its results do not establish safety or effectiveness in patient care.
method: Build 3,078 clinician-annotated stepwise problems from MedQA-USMLE.
Organize each vignette into EMR-aligned findings, impressions, and supporting rationales.
Evaluate LLMs, fine-tune Qwen2.5-7B and 32B, and test robustness and error propagation.
infographic.evidence_signal: ASCENT fine-tuning improved F1 over pre-trained and HuatuoGPT-o1 CoT-trained baselines, primarily through precision gains; the abstract does not report effect sizes.
infographic.watch_item: Errors can propagate across sequential predictions, and evaluation on exam-derived vignettes does not establish real-world clinical reliability.
infographic.paper_title: ASCENT: A Benchmark for Evaluating and Advancing Stepwise Diagnostic Reasoning in Large Language Models on Common Clinical Scenarios

title: A dataset of clinically similar image pairs from citation-linked case reports for medical image retrieval
authors: Guy Shmueli, Keno K. Bressem, Tom Hope
abstract: Retrieving images of patients clinically similar to a given patient can support diagnosis, teaching and research. Training and evaluating retrieval systems requires knowing which images of different patients show the same finding, and existing datasets are small or narrow in scope. We construct PMC-PaIR, a dataset of 86,144 pairs of clinically similar images from 56,013 open-access PubMed Central case reports, which often document rare or challenging presentations. We develop an approach that follows citations, which often link case reports of similar patients. To determine what two linked cases share clinically, it prompts large language models to generate and answer hierarchical questions, from modality to diagnosis and findings, and to match images by caption using the answers. Experts find the pairs highly accurate, and this question-guided approach finds twice as many correct pairs as direct matching. Fine-tuning BiomedCLIP on PMC-PaIR improves retrieval in all modality, anatomy and diagnosis categories tested, for image-only queries and image queries with a short text naming the finding. We release the dataset and the automated pipeline, which can extend PMC-PaIR as new case reports are published.

infographic.key_insight: PMC-PaIR uses citation-linked case reports and question-guided language models to build clinically similar image pairs that improve medical image retrieval.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Retrieving images with similar clinical findings could support teaching, research and diagnostic reference, but clinical benefit was not established.
method: Follow citations between open-access case reports to identify potentially similar patients.
Use hierarchical language-model questions about modality, diagnosis and findings to match images through their captions.
Fine-tune BiomedCLIP on the resulting image pairs and evaluate retrieval.
infographic.evidence_signal: The dataset contains 86,144 image pairs from 56,013 case reports; experts rated pairs highly accurate, question-guided matching yielded twice as many correct pairs as direct matching, and fine-tuning improved retrieval across all tested categories.
infographic.watch_item: Case reports often emphasize rare or challenging presentations, so performance may not generalize to routine clinical imaging.
infographic.paper_title: A dataset of clinically similar image pairs from citation-linked case reports for medical image retrieval

title: Privileged On-Policy Distillation for Calibrated Alzheimer's Diagnosis With Missing Modalities
authors: Vo Minh Khoi Nguyen, Dat Tien Chung, Quang Minh Khoa Le, Duc Khang Nguyen, Le Thien Phuc Nguyen, Hoang Thien Nguyen
abstract: Alzheimer's disease is diagnosed from clinical, biospecimen and imaging evidence, but few patients undergo every test. Because these modalities are complementary, a missing one has many plausible values. Most existing methods leave it out or train on one estimate, so their classifier never sees its other values, and the estimate is never checked against the diagnosis. We address both gaps with on-policy distillation: the model fills in the missing modalities itself, and teachers with information available only in training grade these fills. Our method, Graded Rollout Imputation with Privileged teachers, draws several fills, one modality at a time. An imputation teacher that knows the diagnosis grades each step, bringing the outcome into the imputation as statistical practice recommends. A diagnosis teacher that sees all real modalities supplies a soft target. Trained on fills that vary, the model learns a confidence that reflects what the missing tests leave open, and it diagnoses from a single rollout. On the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative cohort, it outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. On two external cohorts, it remains competitive in discrimination and, even after every method is recalibrated, its calibration error is level with the lowest on both. Added to three of these baselines, the teachers improve each of them. Our method offers a single, well-calibrated model for whatever combination of tests a patient has received.

infographic.key_insight: Privileged training teachers help an Alzheimer's classification model learn from varied imputations of missing tests and produce confidence estimates that reflect missing information.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach could support research toward more reliable predictions when patients have incomplete clinical, biospecimen, or imaging data.
method: Generate multiple candidate fills for missing modalities, one modality at a time.
During training, use a diagnosis-informed teacher to grade fills and a full-data teacher to supply soft diagnostic targets.
At inference, predict from a single imputation rollout without privileged teacher information.
infographic.evidence_signal: On ADNI, the method outperformed state-of-the-art baselines; on two external cohorts, discrimination remained competitive and calibration error matched the lowest after all methods were recalibrated.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report cohort sizes or effect sizes, and prospective validation is needed before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: Privileged On-Policy Distillation for Calibrated Alzheimer's Diagnosis With Missing Modalities

title: Sage-Med: Scaling Medical Multimodal Intelligence
authors: Sage-Med Team, :, Ming Hu, Cheng Tang, Wei Li, Rongbin Li
abstract: Establishing effective scaling laws for medical multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remains a persistent and fundamental challenge. Our systematic evaluation shows that existing medical MLLMs tend to underperform frontier general-purpose MLLMs across a range of medical tasks, while scaling model size primarily improves text capabilities rather than multimodal perception, and enabling reasoning modes fails to close this visual gap. To investigate how medical multimodal intelligence scales in practice, we introduce Sage-Med-Preview, a 35B-parameter medical multimodal model with 3B activated parameters, built by combining stage-specific curation over 322.7 million candidate records with a progressive training curriculum spanning medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning. Across this curriculum, progressive supervised refinement and adaptive reinforcement learning yield consistent stage-wise gains, substantially advancing both specialized visual understanding and medical language capabilities. Evaluated against 77 competing models across 238 clinical tasks spanning 61 public and 13 private multi-center benchmarks in more than 40 modalities, Sage-Med-Preview achieves an average score of 58.26% on the 31 public multimodal benchmarks. It outperforms the state-of-the-art open-source medical model Hulu-Med-235B-A22B at 50.99% and the general scientific model Intern-S2-Preview at 52.24%, and approaches the advanced proprietary model GPT-6.2-Sol across multiple tasks such as comprehensive multimodal understanding, report generation, and visual grounding. Although substantial challenges remain in complex medical reasoning and multi-step clinical workflows, this report provides empirical evidence, actionable data and training recipes, and a rigorous benchmark toward scalable clinical multimodal intelligence.

infographic.key_insight: Sage-Med-Preview reports improved medical multimodal performance through staged training, while the study finds that model size and reasoning modes alone do not close visual capability gaps.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The model could support research into medical image interpretation and report generation, but benchmark results do not establish safety or effectiveness in clinical care.
method: 35B-parameter multimodal model with 3B activated parameters.
Stage-specific data curation from 322.7 million candidate records.
Progressive medical pretraining, staged supervised fine-tuning, and adaptive reinforcement learning.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across an evaluation involving 77 competing models and 238 clinical tasks, Sage-Med-Preview averaged 58.26% on 31 public multimodal benchmarks versus 50.99% for Hulu-Med-235B-A22B and 52.24% for Intern-S2-Preview.
infographic.watch_item: Complex medical reasoning and multi-step clinical workflows remain challenging; prospective clinical validation is needed before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Sage-Med: Scaling Medical Multimodal Intelligence

title: BayesPath: Reliability-Aware Bayesian Reasoning for Whole-Slide Pathology Agents
authors: Bryan Wong, Xun Xu, Jongwoo Kim, Huazhu Fu, Nancy F. Chen, Mun Yong Yi
abstract: Diagnosing whole-slide images (WSIs) requires hypothesis-driven reasoning: pathologists form a differential diagnosis, seek discriminative evidence, weigh its reliability, and stop once it suffices. However, existing training-free WSI agents lack an explicit framework for such reasoning. They typically use a large language model (LLM) to aggregate the region descriptions of a multimodal LLM (MLLM), without a belief over the candidates or regard for the descriptions' reliability. Consequently, a repeated model error counts as independent evidence for an incorrect diagnosis. We introduce BayesPath, a training-free WSI agent that casts the pathologist's Scan-Look-Weigh-Decide process as reliability-aware Bayesian reasoning. An explicit belief over the candidates is updated with each observation through a reliability-aware likelihood and guides where to look next and when to stop. This likelihood corrects for the models' answer bias, discounts correlated observations, and captures diagnostic confusions estimated without labels. The updates form an interpretable evidence trail of how each observation shapes the belief. On five MultiPathQA tasks spanning slide classification and slide VQA, BayesPath achieves the highest average accuracy among training-free agents, 58.6% against 34.1% for the next best, with large gains on slide classification. On identical observations, Bayesian updating outperforms LLM aggregation on average, even with a larger LLM. BayesPath's belief is also better calibrated than naive Bayes, so uncertain cases can be deferred to pathologists. Code is available at https://github.com/bryanwong17/BayesPath

infographic.key_insight: BayesPath improves whole-slide pathology reasoning by updating diagnostic beliefs while accounting for unreliable and correlated AI observations.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Its interpretable evidence trail and better-calibrated uncertainty could support pathology review and flag uncertain cases for pathologists.
method: Uses a training-free Scan–Look–Weigh–Decide workflow to guide region selection and stopping.
Updates candidate beliefs with reliability-aware Bayesian likelihoods.
Corrects model answer bias, discounts correlated observations, and models diagnostic confusions estimated without labels.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five MultiPathQA slide-classification and slide-VQA tasks, BayesPath achieved 58.6% average accuracy versus 34.1% for the next-best training-free agent.
infographic.watch_item: Benchmark gains do not establish clinical readiness; prospective validation and safe deferral thresholds remain necessary.
infographic.paper_title: BayesPath: Reliability-Aware Bayesian Reasoning for Whole-Slide Pathology Agents

title: Did the Model Forecast It, or Already Know It? Evaluating Large Language Models for Novel Drug-Target Prioritisation with a Temporal Knowledge-Graph Oracle
authors: Pui Chung Siu, Yuan Liang, Claudia Cabrera, Mani Mudaliar, Arkaitz Zubiaga
abstract: AI systems increasingly help decide which drug targets enter costly clinical trials. We recast each target-disease hypothesis as a dated event, the pair's first clinical trial. This lets us test whether a language model can forecast such events after its training cutoff, rather than recall events before it. We rebuild a dated biomedical knowledge graph as it stood at the end of each year from 2020 up to its newest version. We then ask six open language models, with and without this graph, which targets will enter a first trial for a disease the next year. Without retrieval, the models rank about as well as trial history, a count of each target's past trials in the same therapeutic area, also after their training cutoffs. Evidence dated before the decision adds at most a small gain, before or after the models' training cutoffs. The newest graph raises five of six models clearly above that baseline, but its paths usually include the answer: the pair's own trial, dated after the decision. Evaluations of target prioritisation should date both features and labels, with evidence from before the decision and outcomes after it.

infographic.key_insight: Apparent gains in drug-target forecasting may reflect access to future trial evidence rather than genuine prediction.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Reliable target prioritisation could inform which hypotheses enter costly clinical trials, but these findings caution against treating model rankings as validated forecasts.
method: Defined each target–disease event as its first clinical trial.
Rebuilt annual biomedical knowledge graphs from 2020 onward.
Evaluated six open language models with and without graph retrieval against a trial-history baseline.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evidence available before the decision added at most small gains, while the newest graph clearly improved five of six models but usually included the target–disease pair’s own future trial.
infographic.watch_item: Date both inputs and outcomes: using evidence recorded after the decision can leak the answer and inflate forecasting performance.
infographic.paper_title: Did the Model Forecast It, or Already Know It? Evaluating Large Language Models for Novel Drug-Target Prioritisation with a Temporal Knowledge-Graph Oracle

title: EATS: Scaling Tool-Use Experience for Medical Reasoning Agents
authors: Mingyuan Li, Tong Jia, Haoran Wang, Wenbo Qi, Ziyuan Yang, Bowen Ma
abstract: Medical reasoning agents combine large language model (LLM) reasoning with clinical workflows and specialized neural tools. However, general-purpose LLMs receive limited training exposure to domain-specific medical tools, and the uncertainty and distributional shifts of neural tool outputs make selecting tools from simple descriptions significantly more challenging than in deterministic settings such as calculators or dictionary lookups. In this paper, we propose EATS, an experience-augmented tool selection strategy that leverages accumulated tool-use trajectories to improve tool selection in medical reasoning agents. EATS constructs a memory of past interactions, including queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback, and retrieves relevant experiences to guide tool selection for new queries. As memory construction does not require ground-truth supervision, EATS scales naturally with test-time experience. We evaluate EATS on tool-augmented medical reasoning tasks, including closed-ended visual question answering and free-form report generation. Experiments on four public datasets, ChestAgentBench, CheXbench, MIMIC-CXR, and SLAKE-VQA, across three multimodal LLMs, Qwen3-VL 2B, Qwen3-VL 32B, and GPT-5.5, show consistent gains in tool selection behavior and downstream medical reasoning performance. Code is available at https://github.com/Limingyuan001/EATS.

infographic.key_insight: EATS improves medical reasoning agents’ tool selection by retrieving relevant past tool-use experiences rather than relying only on tool descriptions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Experience-guided tool use could support medical image question answering and report generation, though clinical benefit is not established.
method: Store queries, tool choices, arguments, and self-evaluated feedback in a memory.
Retrieve relevant experiences to guide tool selection for new queries.
Expand memory with test-time interactions without ground-truth supervision.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent gains in tool selection and downstream performance across four public datasets and three multimodal LLMs, but provides no effect sizes.
infographic.watch_item: Self-evaluated memories may retain incorrect tool-use patterns, warranting independent validation before clinical deployment.
infographic.paper_title: EATS: Scaling Tool-Use Experience for Medical Reasoning Agents
